text: When a long-term architectural change becomes the standard (e.g., ~95% implemented), document the resulting convention as a guideline in the docs and treat deviations from it as bugs.
reason: Signals migration completion, makes the new convention discoverable and enforceable, and removes ambiguity for contributors instead of leaving them to infer the direction from partial adoption.
common_pattern: Documentation and enforcement of a convention once a long-term architectural migration is near-complete or complete: publish the guideline and treat deviations as bugs.

text: When documenting JavaScript override or customization mechanisms, describe load-order and execution-timing dependencies (e.g., module evaluation vs execution after DOMContentLoaded, registration/replacement before vs after DOM load) and their side effects, so developers understand when and whether overrides actually take effect.
reason: The two generalizations are complementary halves of the same documentation requirement: both emphasize explaining timing nuances (before/after DOM load, module evaluation vs hook execution) and their side effects for JS overrides. Merging them yields one complete rule.
scope: JS override/customization documentation, especially framework integrations (e.g., Stimulus)
common_pattern: Documenting JavaScript override/customization mechanisms must explicitly cover timing and load-order dependencies that determine whether overrides take effect.

text: Roadmap documentation should explicitly state the full range of change types it covers—including refactors, removals, architecture work, and cross-cutting improvements—and should include items whose primary category is different (e.g., security) when they provide secondary sustainability or performance benefits, explaining the benefit mechanism.
reason: Merges both generalizations into one coherent documentation rule: clarify roadmap scope and justify inclusion of cross-cutting work with secondary benefits.
common_pattern: Roadmap documentation should explicitly define its scope and include non-feature/cross-cutting work when it is relevant, explaining why it belongs there.

text: When a proposal introduces a database-backed model that overlaps with or replaces an existing Django setting/framework feature (e.g., LANGUAGES), document the existing feature's limitations, the relationship between the new model and the existing feature, and any built-in mechanisms (such as template tags) that depend on the setting and require custom replacements or updates.
reason: Clarifies design rationale, avoids confusion about why the existing feature is not reused directly, and ensures reviewers and implementers account for built-in framework behavior tied to the setting.
common_pattern: Proposals that introduce a database-backed model overlapping with or replacing an existing Django framework setting/feature must document the existing feature's limitations, its relationship to the new model, and the built-in mechanisms that need replacement or updating.

text: In documentation tables with rating or ordinal columns (e.g., Impact, Reach, Complexity), sort rows consistently by a key rating column—prefer Impact first, then Reach—using a consistent direction (high to low).
reason: Readers infer sort order, so inconsistent or missing sorting misleads about prioritization and makes tables harder to scan.
scope: roadmap/documentation tables with rating columns, especially `text/090-sustainability-roadmap.md` improvement tables
common_pattern: Consistently sorting table rows by relevant rating columns to make intended prioritization clear and scannable

text: In RFCs/design docs for multilingual page/site support, specify a URL routing strategy that defaults to language-prefixed paths (e.g., `/en/page`, `/fr/page`) rather than a single shared URL, and optionally allow per-language subdomains as configuration.
reason: Distinct language-prefixed URLs avoid extra cache-server configuration, are search-engine friendly, align with established routing conventions such as Django `i18_patterns`, and allow deployments that prefer per-language subdomains.
common_pattern: Multilingual URL routing strategy must be specified explicitly, defaulting to language-prefixed URLs, with per-language subdomains as an optional configuration.

text: In headless support RFCs, define headless as the CMS no longer rendering or serving HTML; server-rendered HTML delivered via htmx/hotwire/AHAH is not headless unless a separate renderer sends it to the client without Wagtail directly handling the request. Treat API documentation/OpenAPI schemas as useful but non-blocking, and document known workarounds or alternatives for features listed as unsupported.
reason: Prevents ambiguity in RFC scope and keeps headless work focused on functional parity while still giving readers concrete paths for unsupported features.
common_pattern: Wagtail headless-support RFC/API guidance: define headless as no server-rendered HTML, evaluate backend/API responsibility separately from frontend rendering, preserve template feature parity through queryable REST API exposure, and document unsupported-feature workarounds while treating API documentation as useful but non-blocking.

text: Wagtail RFC/design documents (especially API RFCs under `text/`) must go beyond conceptual motivation or an explanation of why a pattern is interesting: include the concrete, actionable specification/design of the proposed API behavior that reviewers need to evaluate and implement it. Additionally, make the `Documentation efforts` section enumerate all documentation work the proposal requires (reference docs, user guides, tutorials), not only release-specific upgrade or migration notes.
reason: RFCs are used to evaluate and implement proposals, so motivation-only sections leave the design underspecified, and an incomplete documentation scope hides required work from implementers and users.
scope: Wagtail API RFCs / project RFC and design documentation in `text/`
common_pattern: RFC/design documents must not stop at partial coverage (motivation-only or release-notes-only); each section should fully specify its remit — concrete design details for the proposal and the complete documentation scope it entails.

text: Wagtail RFCs under `text/` must be explicit decision documents: state the specific goal/objectives and benefits up front; enumerate all proposed changes, including minor default/behavior changes; populate the Open Questions section with concrete unresolved items and give each a `Proposed resolution` (adopt, defer, reject), deferring only non-blocking/tangential concerns; use definitive, concrete language for settled decisions instead of hedges or soft recommendations; and document alternatives or an exit strategy for long-lived or developer-facing abstractions.
reason: Keeps RFCs actionable and unambiguous for reviewers, surfaces scope and unresolved decisions early, prevents hidden design commitments, and avoids locking the project into unjustified or under-specified abstractions.
common_pattern: RFC/proposal documentation quality: all generalizations specify structural or rhetorical requirements for Wagtail RFCs under `text/`, requiring them to be explicit, complete, decision-oriented, and actionable for reviewers.

text: In Wagtail RFCs and design docs, describe UI features by their established product names rather than by implementation technology, and explicitly state the execution context (Wagtail admin interface, public frontend, or both) for new JavaScript or static assets.
reason: Keeps documentation focused on user-facing behaviour, reduces ambiguity about where a script applies, and avoids tying terminology to implementation details that may change.
common_pattern: Wagtail RFC and design documentation should be precise, reader-oriented, and connected to existing conventions: describe features by established product names, clarify execution context, and cross-reference related discussions or unified mechanisms.

text: In documentation/examples for Django `LANGUAGES` / `WAGTAIL_CONTENT_LANGUAGES`, wrap human-readable language names in gettext `_()` to demonstrate and encourage translatable strings.
reason: Language labels are user-facing text and should be translatable; examples set the convention readers will copy.
common_pattern: Wagtail internationalisation configuration design: how locale/language settings and Locale records should be defined, named, and kept consistent, so content languages are clearly distinguished from Django's UI/backend language settings.

text: In admin-facing design/RFC docs, describe each mutually exclusive redirect option by writing out its user-visible behavior with concrete before/after URL examples (and qualify prefix matching as opt-in), instead of relying on terse symbols such as a trailing asterisk.
reason: Explicit descriptions and examples make behavior understandable to non-technical users and prevent readers from assuming all redirects match nested paths by default.
common_pattern: Redirect handling in Wagtail admin: how prefix matching is represented, validated, and documented. The cluster splits into distinct sub-patterns — (a) encoding prefix matching via trailing '*' (PR#34, rules 4-5), (b) excluding self-referential redirects to avoid loops (PR#34, rule 1), (c) accounting for i18n-prefixed URLs in path comparison (PR#93, rules 2-3), and (d) documenting redirect options explicitly (PR#34, rules 6-7).

text: In documentation prose, use official capitalization for technology, framework, and library names (e.g., 'Sass' not 'SASS', 'JavaScript' not 'Javascript', 'Alpine', 'Stimulus', 'React'). Additionally, treat project/organization names as proper nouns: use the official capitalization ('Wagtail', not 'wagtail') and the possessive apostrophe form ('Wagtail's', not 'Wagtails').
reason: Consistent, correct capitalization and proper-noun forms improve documentation quality and correctly identify named technologies and projects.
common_pattern: Capitalization conventions in documentation (proper technology names and heading case style)

text: In roadmap RFCs (e.g., `text/*-roadmap-updates.md`) and roadmap sections, keep the RFC body focused on the near-term core proposal/specification: either omit implementation roadmaps or place them in an appendix explicitly labeled as a proposed roadmap, and exclude speculative or non-near-term items (e.g., components already slated for replacement, advanced third-party customization/extension APIs) by moving them to a separate planning/roadmap document. Each roadmap item should include a concise title, the intended use case/motivation, and links to all relevant tracking artifacts: include both the tracking issue/RFC and the associated implementation PR where applicable (e.g., `[Item](issue-url) & [PR #number](pr-url)`). When a feature area has multiple complementary trackers, list each with a short annotation of what it covers rather than replacing an existing resource that still serves a distinct purpose. Only list items with a defined target release or sufficiently clear scope; defer items tied only to an indeterminate `Future` release.
reason: Roadmaps are volatile planning artifacts that can distract from the RFC decision and go stale; requiring motivation, links, and explicit tracker scopes makes proposals understandable and traceable, while excluding uncommitted or speculative items prevents them from being merged as if committed and keeps the RFC focused on near-term core priorities.
common_pattern: Documentation conventions for roadmap RFCs under `text/` — how roadmap items should be structured, linked to tracking artifacts, annotated with status/rationale, and versioned relative to releases.

text: In roadmap RFCs, record partial progress on an item (e.g., completed sub-scope) in the item's Notes rather than only its high-level status, and when an item is de-prioritized or moved to `Future`, include the explicit rationale, such as higher-priority work identified during the relevant release cycle.
reason: Status changes alone do not explain why priorities changed, and readers need visibility into partial progress — not just whether an item is Done/Ongoing/TBC — plus the release-cycle context that justifies precedence decisions.
common_pattern: Documentation conventions for roadmap RFCs under `text/` — how roadmap items should be structured, linked to tracking artifacts, annotated with status/rationale, and versioned relative to releases.

text: In RFC/spec documentation, explicitly state the supported commenting granularity for nested block types (e.g., block-level vs. field-within-StructBlock) and keep content-path examples consistent with that stated granularity.
reason: Prevents documenting capabilities the addressing scheme cannot support and removes ambiguity about which nested fields or blocks can receive comments.
common_pattern: Commenting/annotation addressing in nested StreamField content must be tied to revision-stable content paths — enabling comment anchoring at any hierarchy level where addressing is reliable, and constraining or documenting granularity where it is not.

text: Framework/library adoption RFCs must explicitly document scope and non-goals, future compatibility with complementary libraries, external reuse/importability, and a 'Why not [framework]' trade-off section covering the learning burden of the new framework, any auxiliary libraries/tooling, and existing stack knowledge that remains required.
reason: Ensures readers understand what the adoption does and does not replace, preserves future optionality, surfaces reuse/decoupling requirements, and accurately documents adoption costs such as learning burden.
scope: RFC/design documentation for frontend framework adoption
common_pattern: Guidance for RFCs that adopt a new frontend framework/library: make scope, trade-offs, and architectural constraints explicit before adoption.

text: Whenever template override discovery is added, document the exact lookup directories and their precedence.
reason: Users need to know where to place overriding templates, especially when the discovery path is an implementation detail that could otherwise be surprising.
common_pattern: Conventions for template override discovery: use a cascading, feature-level lookup namespace and document the lookup directories and precedence.

text: In roadmap/RFC documentation, distinguish 'deprecate' from 'remove': do not schedule deprecation in the same release that introduces its replacement; require replacement feature parity and a clear migration path before announcing removal; and defer or omit items whose scope or timeline is undecided. For RFCs that migrate, merge, replace, or deprecate repositories/packages or widely used resources, also specify external coordination and dependency handling: notify and audit affected external repos/issues, provide a transitional compatibility mechanism with clear ownership, state the deprecation/end-of-life path, and tie any deadline to the availability of required external features rather than an arbitrary date.
reason: Prevents ambiguous roadmap commitments, avoids premature removal, and ensures migrations account for external dependencies, compatibility, and stakeholder coordination.
common_pattern: Migration, merge, replacement, and deprecation RFCs must account for external dependencies and stakeholders: coordination/notification, auditing affected external issues/PRs, transitional compatibility, deprecation/end-of-life path, and deadlines tied to external feature availability.

text: Breaking changes to default behavior must be documented in developer-facing documentation (e.g., dev docs and release notes) with a clear migration path: advance warning/deprecation, an explicit opt-in/opt-out or compatibility flag, and exact configuration/steps to restore the previous behavior. A user-guide mention alone is not sufficient.
reason: Developers rely on dev docs as the canonical technical reference, and affected users need a predictable, copy-pasteable migration path rather than having to reverse-engineer how to opt out or restore prior behavior.
common_pattern: Breaking changes to established default behavior must be handled explicitly: documented in developer-facing docs and accompanied by a clear migration path (warning/deprecation, opt-in/opt-out or compatibility flag, and instructions to restore prior behavior).

text: Autosave specifications must document both integration and UX. RFCs/roadmap sections introducing autosave must document how it integrates with related features: how revisions behave under autosave, and whether save mechanisms for inline/front-end editing, snippets, arbitrary Django models, or fields without Telepath adapters can reuse the same autosave mechanism. Autosave UX specs must define save-state messaging and navigation safety: replace generic “unsaved changes” warnings with a relative “Last saved … ago” indicator (preferably in the page header) and an explicit “unpublished changes”/saved-but-not-fully-saved state, keep these statuses meaningful during validation errors or edit conflicts, and retain unload/navigation-away confirmation while a background save may be in flight across the autosave interval and request round-trip.
reason: Merges the documentation requirement for autosave integration with the UX specification requirement for save-state messaging and navigation safety.
scope: autosave RFCs, roadmaps, and UX specs
common_pattern: Autosave UX/specification: explicitly define save-state communication and navigation safety rather than relying on a binary unsaved/saved model.

text: Concurrent-save/overwrite safety: Save/autosave endpoints must exchange a version marker and detect stale/conflicting submissions. Return the server-persisted revision/timestamp/counter after a successful save, and require the client to send its last-known marker on the next save request. On edit/save, derive the submitted revision from `overwrite_revision_id` when present, otherwise from the optional `loaded_revision_id` (the revision loaded when the form was rendered); compare a version discriminator (e.g. the revision's `created_at`, overwrite counter, or UUID). If the submitted revision is stale (mismatch with the object's latest revision ID) and there is no explicit force-overwrite flag, treat the submission as a validation error and re-render the form without saving rather than silently overwriting. When a flow may overwrite another user's newer changes, require an explicit acknowledgement control (e.g., a checkbox confirming the user knows they may overwrite others' changes) before allowing the operation, and offer a diff preview (modal or linked view) comparing the user's current/original version with the latest version before confirmation. Do not rely solely on interval-based polling/ping notifications: after a successful save/publish, notify the user if their action overwrote or skipped another user's newer revision, since polling gaps can miss revisions created shortly before the save.
reason: Merges version-marker exchange, stale-revision rejection, explicit acknowledgement/diff-preview for destructive overwrites, and post-save overwrite notification into a single concurrent-save/overwrite safety rule.
scope: global save/autosave endpoints and destructive/overwriting save flows, including Wagtail admin edit/autosave save-conflict handling
common_pattern: Save/autosave endpoints should exchange a version marker: the server returns the persisted revision/timestamp/counter after a successful save, and the client sends its last-known marker on the next save request so the server can detect missed, out-of-order, or stale writes.

text: For every API resource, define exactly one canonical URL and construct paths with explicit parent resource identifiers: include the actual parent ID (e.g. `/api/pages/<page-id>/revisions/<revision-id>/`), never an implicit placeholder such as `-`. Endpoints that act on a parent (e.g. creating a child page) must carry the parent context in the path/query (e.g. `POST /api/pages/<parent-page-id>/add_child/?type=<app.Model>`). Alternate or alias URL shapes that could resolve the same resource—including wildcard-parent/child-alias combinations such as `-` with `head`—must not return the resource payload or an undefined 404; instead redirect them to the canonical URL (preferably HTTP 301), or explicitly reject them if redirects are not supported.
reason: Required context such as parent page ID and page type is not carried in child/revision payloads, so it must appear explicitly in the endpoint. At the same time, each API resource needs one unambiguous canonical location so clients do not depend on undocumented aliases or duplicate representations.
common_pattern: Canonical URL policy for API resources: exactly one canonical URL per resource, with alternate/alias URL shapes explicitly handled via redirect to canonical or rejection instead of serving duplicate representations.

text: For ephemeral state tracked by a periodic heartbeat with a staleness timeout, rely on ping plus expiry for cleanup by default; add an explicit release/delete endpoint only when expiry latency is unacceptable for real-time feedback or immediate cleanup is required. Use server-side expiry as the source of truth: do not rely on client-side lifecycle events (`visibilitychange`, `focus`/`blur`) or periodic pings for correctness of session/editing-session lifecycle. If periodic pings/timers exist, suspend them when the document is hidden or idle only as a best-effort optimization.
reason: Heartbeat plus timeout provides a single, client-event-independent removal path and reduces API surface; an explicit release endpoint is justified only for real-time responsiveness. Client lifecycle events are inconsistently emitted across platforms, so server-side expiry avoids missed cleanup without relying on unreliable client signals.
common_pattern: Client-side session lifecycle should not depend on unreliable browser lifecycle events or periodic pings for correctness; server-side expiry should be the source of truth, and client-side timer suspension is at most a best-effort optimization.

text: Expiring or releasable locks must provide an explicit prolongation/keep-alive mechanism so active sessions can signal they are still editing — e.g., a periodic frontend timer (`window.setInterval`) calling a `keep_lock` endpoint such as `current_url/keep_lock`. This keep-alive is a client-side signal and remains best-effort; server-side expiry is still the source of truth.
reason: Without a keep-alive signal the lock may be released while a user is still editing, defeating the purpose of page locking; a periodic request-based refresh avoids needing websockets.
common_pattern: Design of expiring lock/transient-resource lifetimes: configurable timeout measured from last activity, plus an explicit keep-alive/prolongation mechanism to prevent premature release.

text: Design API action endpoints around the resource identified in the URL. Page-level actions that do not involve revisions use /api/pages/<page-id>/<action>/ (e.g. POST /api/pages/<page-id>/unpublish/), while revision-specific actions are nested under the revision (e.g. /api/pages/<page-id>/revisions/<revision-id>/moderation/<action>/). When an action operates entirely on an existing resource identified in the URL, do not require request body content; the operation acts on that resource's state or content. Keep URL semantics aligned with the underlying model/view implementation.
reason: Prevents endpoints from implying a different resource than they operate on, avoids redundant payloads, and makes the action's source of truth explicit through the URL resource identifier.
scope: API action endpoint design (URL scoping and request body)
common_pattern: RESTful HTTP endpoint design for resources with state transitions/actions: prefer standard HTTP methods and field updates over proliferating custom action sub-endpoints, and keep action endpoints minimal.

text: Only add core/framework API surface when it requires genuine framework-level integration and provides concrete functional benefit. When a feature's full workflow depends on a third-party package, keep core limited to a minimal integration hook and let the package own the UI/workflow. For trivial, site/framework-specific, consistency-only, or context-specialized features, prefer documenting a snippet, providing concrete use-case samples, or using an existing general-purpose solution over adding new namespaces, attributes, APIs, or contrib-style restructuring. Any added migration burden or API surface must be justified by functional benefit.
reason: Minimizes the core API surface and migration burden, avoids maintaining functionality that does not need framework support, and lets third-party packages or site implementers own workflows they are better positioned to innovate on.
scope: Wagtail core extension/API design and general API design
common_pattern: Scope decisions about what belongs in Wagtail core versus third-party packages or documentation: core should only own functionality that genuinely requires framework-level integration, delegating site-specific or package-dependent workflows elsewhere.

text: Decide how to model a new asset/media type based on its processing characteristics: if the format is always converted to the existing type's output (e.g., SVG always rasterized to PNG), integrate it into the existing module and admin pipeline; if it has fundamentally different processing, security, or storage behavior (e.g., vector SVG vs raster), model it as a separate content type. In Wagtail, implement SVG support outside core raster `wagtail.images` handling, e.g. as a separate content type in a `contrib`/third-party app with an 'SVG images' admin section, keeping regular image handling unchanged. In all cases, keep media-type support composable so projects can enable both types and choose per use case.
reason: Separates concerns when behavior genuinely differs, avoids duplicating user-facing infrastructure when the final representation is the same, keeps regular image handling unchanged while giving SVG-specific behavior its own home, and lets projects supporting both vector and raster formats select the right one per use case.
common_pattern: A conditional decision rule for how to model a new asset/media type: whether it has fundamentally distinct characteristics (needs its own content type) or is always converted to the existing type's output (should be integrated into the existing module).

text: Design Wagtail image-rendering template tags to preserve their existing default output semantics while adding explicit, opt-in, format-aware APIs — such as arguments, modifiers, or dedicated tags — so templates can vary rendering for vector/raster or other special formats (e.g. SVG, animated GIF) without manual `{% if %}` branching. Apply sensible format-aware defaults where possible and avoid exposing format/filter combinations that force template authors to remember compatibility rules. For SVG support in `wagtail.images` specifically, prefer vector-native attribute manipulation (`width`, `height`, `viewBox`, `preserveAspectRatio`, root-group fill/bgcolor) over rasterization; deliver SVG renditions by default and provide an opt-in flag such as `preserveSVG` to skip rasterization-requiring filters when vector preservation is desired, while still allowing developers to opt into rasterization when style fidelity is more important.
reason: Merges the general template-tag API design guidance with the specific SVG implementation guidance: keep defaults backward-compatible, provide opt-in format-aware escape hatches, avoid manual branching and incompatible format/filter combinations, and preserve SVG vectors unless rasterization is explicitly requested.
scope: Wagtail images template API and SVG support
common_pattern: Special handling for SVG images in Wagtail, covering security (sanitization, safe serving), rendering (vector-native transformations, opt-in rasterization), and architecture (separate content type).

text: In Wagtail's search query API, prefer documenting and composing existing primitives instead of adding special-case or dedicated query classes when the behavior can be expressed that way. For score adjustments, express branch score changes through the existing relative `Boost` query rather than adding absolute constant-score classes such as `ConstantScore`, because absolute constant scores depend on unknown data magnitudes and create ambiguous composition with other score components; `Boost` already handles scaling a branch's score and zeroing it out. If an explicit query class is added to replace a legacy implicit input/sentinel (e.g. `MatchAll()` for `None`), preserve the legacy input when maintenance cost is low, document the explicit class as the preferred API for new code, and provide a clear migration/deprecation path rather than leaving ambiguous or indistinguishable semantics.
reason: Keeps the Wagtail query API surface smaller and avoids ambiguity from overlapping query classes. `ConstantScore` is only reliable when every branch is constant-scored, while `Boost` already handles relative scaling and zeroing. When replacing legacy implicit inputs, balance backwards compatibility against API clarity with a documented migration path.
common_pattern: Search query score modifiers should rely on relative Boost semantics, and their documentation must explain how they transform child queries/terms rather than only describing final score effects.

text: Store autosave/draft form state separately from validated model instances and revisions using a dedicated `FormState` record (or distinct temporary WIP revision type). Autosave must not create/update the underlying model instance or trigger validation/workflows; full validation, revision creation, and workflow triggers happen only on explicit Save/Publish/Schedule/Submit. Persist in-progress form state in a `FormState` model that round-trips with Django forms: construct/save it from form submission data (QueryDict-like, multi-value) and restore it by binding the stored data through the normal ModelForm path, not by custom field assignment. On a valid save, delete the associated `FormState`; if retained, resolve editor load conflicts by comparing `FormState` and `Revision` recency and using the newer one. Temporary WIP records are scoped per user and excluded from normal revision listings. For create views (e.g. Wagtail admin), do not persist the model until the form is valid; represent in-progress creation as a `FormState` linked by `content_type` (optionally with parent page/object ID to scope by location). On reload, hydrate the create form from the latest matching `FormState` (matched by `content_type` and user), otherwise show an empty form; surface these instance-less `FormState`s in a dedicated dashboard section whose entries link back to the create view and preload the saved form state. For edit/autosave, resume by preferring the latest `FormState` for the current user and `(content_type, object_id)`, falling back to the latest `Revision` only when no `FormState` exists. If loading a `Revision` as an object fails because its serialized data is incompatible, fall back to `FormState` when available. Keep `FormState` lookup user-scoped for now, but structure it so user scoping can later be relaxed to load the latest `FormState` for the model instance regardless of user, enabling future concurrent editing. For collaborative-editing implementations, persist incomplete content as a real shared draft and expose draft/autosave state (e.g. `FormState`) to any user with the appropriate permission—not just its creator—and ensure the underlying page/field data model is serialisable for collaboration-friendly diff exchange (e.g. CRDT/OT-compatible websocket updates). This enables restoring incomplete or invalid forms without running validation, avoids crashes when model definitions change, and reduces implementation risk by reusing existing form behavior.
reason: Merges the broad autosave/FormState lifecycle and collaborative-editing guidance with the complementary Django-form round-tripping implementation detail; both describe the same `FormState` persistence and restoration approach for Wagtail admin create/edit/autosave.
scope: Wagtail admin create/edit/autosave, `FormState` model and Django form round-tripping, revision fallback, dashboard discoverability, and collaborative editing foundations
common_pattern: Wagtail admin editing design: autosave/draft form state must be modeled and stored separately from validated model revisions, with validation, revision creation, and workflow triggers reserved for explicit save/publish actions — plus revision-conflict detection on save/edit endpoints.

text: When a behavior is a variant of an existing string value, prefer encoding the variant in the string syntax with validation instead of adding a standalone boolean/checkbox field. If internal code needs to distinguish the variant, persist a derived flag on save so the variant does not need to be re-parsed from the string. In Wagtail redirect admin forms and models specifically, encode prefix matching with a trailing `*` on the path fields, and apply the same convention to the destination path, where an omitted `*` means redirect all matches to the exact target. Validate with a regex that the `*` only appears at the end.
reason: Reduces schema and UI surface area while keeping the variant explicit and validated, provides a stable internal representation for downstream code, and makes source/destination wildcard behavior symmetric in Wagtail redirects.
scope: global; Wagtail redirect admin forms and models
common_pattern: Encode semantic variants in existing string syntax with validation, and persist a derived flag when internal code needs to distinguish the variant without re-parsing.

text: When adding relations to Wagtail's shared Page model, avoid coupling core models to optional or cross-cutting functionality (e.g., RFC 45 Workflow association): model such features as a separate model linked to Page via OneToOneField rather than adding a ForeignKey directly on Page. For any new relation field or reverse accessor on a shared/core model like Page, check whether the field name or reverse accessor can collide with fields already defined on user subclasses; prefer a namespaced name, or set related_name='+' when no reverse accessor is needed.
reason: A direct ForeignKey on Page couples core models to optional features, risks field-name clashes with existing projects, and introduces side effects in page copy and revision workflows. Downstream Wagtail projects may already use common field names such as workflow, so new core relations can introduce migration/model clashes or unintended accessor-name conflicts.
common_pattern: For optional or cross-cutting functionality on Wagtail pages, use a separate link model connected to Page via OneToOneField instead of adding a ForeignKey field directly on Page; this avoids field-name clashes and keeps core Page copy/revision workflows unaffected.

text: Headless support (e.g., Wagtail) must specify and implement end-to-end URL routing for pages: document link-handling edge cases in the RFC/design (missing page-serving routes, multi-site/default-site API routing); provide an unpaginated, URL-only endpoint to enumerate all page URLs for static frontend builds; allow `Page.serve` to be overridden to return an API response for one-to-one page-URL-to-frontend-route mapping; and make admin live/preview links point to the frontend URL, e.g. by overriding `Page.get_url_parts`.
reason: Headless setups bypass standard Wagtail serving URLs, so broken links, incorrect multi-site routing, and poor editor preview experiences occur unless routing, enumeration, serving, and admin links are designed together.
common_pattern: Requirements for Wagtail headless support to handle page URL/link routing end-to-end, covering design documentation, page enumeration, page serving, and admin preview/live URLs.

text: For headless/static-generation integrations, fetch shared data in bulk at build time (e.g., retrieve the full redirect list once) and prefer a single consolidated GraphQL query per page over many REST calls, rather than querying redirects or page data per request.
reason: Reduces request overhead, avoids many round trips, simplifies data aggregation, and supports static-generation and CDN workflows.
scope: Headless data-fetching and redirects integration guidance
common_pattern: In headless/static-generation integrations, avoid per-page or per-request data fetching; instead fetch shared data in bulk at build time and use consolidated queries rather than many separate API calls.

text: For headless access to private or password-protected pages, design authentication to avoid sending raw passwords or shared secrets via request body or query parameters: support a namespaced HTTP header for CMS-side verification, and for static-site/frontend-owned authentication, expose the password hash and hashing details to the frontend. Document this alternative in the relevant private-pages/API section.
reason: A namespaced header avoids URL/log/cache leakage of secrets, while exposing hashes and hashing metadata lets SSG or frontend-owned auth systems verify access without receiving or forwarding the raw shared secret.
scope: Headless API authentication for private pages, especially RFC 100 Private Pages / Wagtail-style CMS
common_pattern: Headless private-page authentication should support secure credential flows that avoid exposing raw passwords/shared secrets in URLs, logs, or caches, covering both CMS-side header exchange and frontend-owned/static-site hash verification.

text: When enumerating the built-in actions for the permission registry, include a basic `view` (read) action alongside actions such as `edit`, `delete`, and `create`.
reason: Viewing is a fundamental permission operation and a generic permissions API should be able to test read/view access just like other actions.
common_pattern: Design of Wagtail's permission registry API: canonical action naming tied to Django permission codenames, one tester class per action/mode, centralized mixin-aware logic, and completeness/documentation of the built-in action set.

text: Enforce required-on-save validation via a generic `required_on_save` attribute on the model field (e.g. `required_on_save = True`) rather than a panel subclass. `FieldPanel` (and other admin panels) should accept an optional panel-level `required_on_save` argument that takes precedence when provided, otherwise falling back to the bound model field's attribute. The attribute must be generic (usable by any field, not title-specific) — set it on the Wagtail page `title` field so draft pages still carry a title for page listings.
reason: Removes dependence on specialized panel classes (such as `TitleFieldPanel`), ensures fields like `title` remain required even when projects use a plain `FieldPanel`, and lets user-defined fields reuse the same mechanism. The explicit panel-argument-over-field-attribute precedence gives a single, predictable resolution order.
common_pattern: All four generalizations describe the same design decision from PR#104: replacing a panel-subclass-specific mechanism (`TitleFieldPanel`) with a generic `required_on_save` attribute on the model field, optionally overridable per-panel, and applying it to the Wagtail page `title` field.

text: Before adding new storage or records for autosave/editing-session state, check whether an existing session/revision model (e.g. Wagtail's EditingSession) already holds similar fields, and extend or rework it instead of creating a parallel model.
reason: Avoids duplicated state, keeps editing-session lifecycle concerns together, and reduces model sprawl.
common_pattern: All generalizations concern the design and documentation of autosave/editing-session architecture in the Wagtail CMS ecosystem — specifically, validating new autosave state against existing session/revision infrastructure and documenting how related features integrate with the same mechanism.

text: Enforce permissions using the platform's existing model permission system (add/change/delete) and place permission checks in the operations/actions layer so that all consumers (API, admin views, management commands, CLI) share the same enforcement. Do not introduce ad-hoc access controls, and do not rely on permission checks existing only in transport/view handlers.
reason: Reuses the platform's authorization model so permissions stay consistent and administrable, and centralizes enforcement so consumers call operations that already enforce permissions instead of duplicating or forgetting checks.
common_pattern: Authorization/permission handling for CMS features: where permission checks are enforced, and how permission semantics and permission-denied states are surfaced to users. The cluster splits into two clear sub-patterns — (a) enforcement location/mechanism, and (b) documentation and denial UX.

text: Workflow validations must target genuinely invalid states (not legitimate editorial actions) and, when a validation would block a valid manual workflow, provide an opt-out mechanism instead of enforcing it unconditionally.
reason: Validation examples and enforcement should reflect real workflow semantics; blocking legitimate manual workflows (e.g., pre-creating redirects) harms usability, so an opt-out preserves valid use cases. This merges the documentation-accuracy and enforcement-flexibility aspects seen across PRs.
common_pattern: Workflow validation logic and its documentation should focus on genuinely invalid states and accommodate legitimate manual workflows rather than blocking them unconditionally.

text: Keyboard shortcuts must mirror the visible UI state and affordances: expose actions through discoverable controls (e.g., dropdown menu options) rather than hidden modifier-key shortcuts, and enable a shortcut only when its associated action button is rendered or available.
reason: Aligning shortcuts with visible UI controls preserves accessibility, discoverability, and consistency, and prevents shortcuts from triggering actions that are hidden or unavailable.
common_pattern: Keyboard shortcuts must remain aligned with visible, discoverable UI affordances and the current UI state: expose actions through standard controls rather than hidden modifier-key shortcuts, and enable shortcuts only when the corresponding action is available.

text: For API resource endpoints, keep create/update request payloads structurally consistent with the corresponding resource representation: preserve the same metadata/content nesting and follow the project's meta/non-meta convention (metadata at the top level, content nested under a dedicated `content` object) rather than flattening content fields.
reason: Keeps request and response schemas symmetric, prevents inconsistent field flattening, and gives clients an unambiguous distinction between resource metadata and resource content.
common_pattern: API resource design should keep request/response payload structure consistent, especially around metadata/content separation, and expose independently editable nested parts through dedicated sub-resource endpoints.

text: When a nested part of a resource (e.g., page `content`) is independently editable, expose a dedicated sub-resource endpoint supporting `PUT`/`PATCH` for that part rather than requiring creation or update of the parent resource.
reason: Allows partial updates via `PATCH` and makes content-only edits simpler without requiring full parent-resource creation.
common_pattern: API resource design should keep request/response payload structure consistent, especially around metadata/content separation, and expose independently editable nested parts through dedicated sub-resource endpoints.

text: In revision API responses, put revision metadata under a `meta` object and expose content fields at the top level, mirroring the corresponding page payload outside `meta`; do not wrap content in a generic `content` object, so GET responses match create payloads and swapping in the page's `meta` reconstructs the page representation at that revision.
reason: A generic `content` wrapper makes the API contract ambiguous, while separating `meta` from top-level content keeps revision responses consistent with page/create payloads and reusable by clients.
common_pattern: Revision API representation: separate revision metadata under `meta`, keep page/content fields at the top level rather than wrapped in `content`, align revision responses with page/create payloads, and name the related meta-field set consistently.

text: Model distinct entity state changes as separate immutable event records linked to the entity, each with its own identifier and timestamp. Attributes that are invariant across all events for an entity (e.g., a timestamp shared by all events for one revision) should be stored on the parent entity, not duplicated on each event record.
reason: Separate event records capture distinct events at different times, while storing invariant attributes on the parent avoids duplication and inconsistency.
common_pattern: Event and metadata modeling conventions for entities in a schema/API: how to structure event records and name their metadata fields.

text: For optional text/note fields, default to plain text and only introduce rich text when there is a clear need; when rich text input is required in the CMS, use the built-in Draftail (WYSIWYG) editor rather than Markdown.
reason: Plain text avoids unnecessary complexity, and Draftail gives content editors a familiar WYSIWYG experience, whereas Markdown is developer-centric and confusing for non-technical CMS users.
common_pattern: Design principles for CMS rich text input fields: default to the simplest viable input type, prefer CMS-native editors over developer-centric formats, and ensure restricted rich text field/block types preserve routine editorial flexibility (documenting representative use cases in RFCs).

text: Expose block lifecycle events as before/after hooks around operations (add, delete, move) rather than only post-operation events. In the Wagtail RFC, use `tree:beforeDelete` instead of only `tree:delete`, and expose both `tree:beforeAdd` and `tree:afterAdd` instead of only `tree:add`.
reason: Before hooks enable validation, cancellation, setup, and state preparation before mutation; relying only on after-the-fact events makes timing and cleanup unreliable.
scope: global, with Wagtail-specific event names as concrete example
common_pattern: Lifecycle event APIs for block operations should provide both before and after hooks (not just after-the-fact events), with event names encoding the timing (e.g., tree:beforeDelete, tree:beforeAdd, tree:afterAdd).

text: For Wagtail's StreamField/InlinePanel admin UI, implement block lifecycle events using React component lifecycle stages (mount/update/unmount) rather than defining custom Wagtail-specific block lifecycle events.
reason: React already provides a built-in component lifecycle, so aligning block events to it avoids duplicate lifecycle concepts, reduces custom lifecycle maintenance, and keeps event timing consistent with the framework.
scope: Wagtail admin frontend architecture using React
common_pattern: Reuse the UI framework's built-in component lifecycle for block lifecycle events instead of creating a parallel Wagtail-specific block lifecycle.

text: Render StreamField/InlinePanel block action bars inside the block's interactive area rather than outside/above the block boundary.
reason: External above-block action bars appear detached from the block and make intensive editing or bulk operations error-prone because users must hover into the block and then move outside to hit the action. An in-block action bar is directly targetable and keeps the action associated with the block. This supersedes the earlier above-block layout proposal.
common_pattern: Placement of action bars for StreamField/InlinePanel editor blocks relative to the block content and interactive area.

text: Register widget initialisers through the shared `registerWidgetInit` helper rather than attaching per-widget `DOMContentLoaded` listeners. `registerWidgetInit` must handle DOM-ready timing: invoke the initialiser immediately when the DOM is already loaded, otherwise attach a `DOMContentLoaded` listener.
reason: Deferred/async scripts may execute after `DOMContentLoaded` has already fired, so a per-widget listener registered later may never run. Centralizing readiness logic in `registerWidgetInit` avoids missed or duplicate initialization.
common_pattern: All three generalizations converge on the same DOM-ready initialization pattern: widget scripts should register through a shared `registerWidgetInit` helper, and that helper should account for deferred/async script timing by checking whether the DOM is already loaded before falling back to `DOMContentLoaded`.

text: In the Wagtail admin page explorer, surface auxiliary page-like records (e.g. redirects) directly in the page list as non-page entries rather than only via a separate icon or management screen. Render these entries with a more compact row height than real pages to distinguish them and reduce visual clutter, and provide a visibility toggle so users can hide them.
reason: Listing redirects inline keeps them discoverable and avoids forgotten redirect clutter, while compact rows plus a toggle keep them visually separable from real pages and let users control noise.
scope: Wagtail admin page explorer UI design
common_pattern: Design guidance for surfacing auxiliary/non-page records (e.g. redirects) in the Wagtail admin page explorer: integrate them into the page list itself while visually de-emphasizing and allowing them to be hidden.

text: When defining redirect path normalization or comparison (e.g. circular redirect checks, old_path vs normalised link), account for i18n-prefixed URLs rather than assuming raw paths are directly comparable.
reason: Wagtail's i18n support can prefix URLs with locale codes; ignoring these prefixes in redirect validation or normalization may cause incorrect redirect detection or behaviour.
scope: Wagtail redirect path handling with i18n
common_pattern: Redirect handling in Wagtail admin: how prefix matching is represented, validated, and documented. The cluster splits into distinct sub-patterns — (a) encoding prefix matching via trailing '*' (PR#34, rules 4-5), (b) excluding self-referential redirects to avoid loops (PR#34, rule 1), (c) accounting for i18n-prefixed URLs in path comparison (PR#93, rules 2-3), and (d) documenting redirect options explicitly (PR#34, rules 6-7).

text:
In a single-segment rich text format, allow `
` as an optional inline element, but enforce a limit on the number of line breaks so users cannot simulate paragraphs inside the segment block.
reason: Manual line breaks are useful for controlling text flow (e.g. headings), but unlimited breaks would let users fake paragraph content and violate the single-segment/single-block constraint.
scope: Rich text segment block / single-segment rich text field design
common_pattern:
Both sub-patterns concern handling of line breaks: one prescribes source-level semantic line breaks for RFC markdown docs, the other constrains inline `
` line breaks in a single-segment rich text format. Gen 2 and Gen 3 are complementary halves of one markdown convention (each sentence on its own line, not wrapped mid-sentence); Gen 1 is a related-but-distinct data-format constraint.

text: For configurable workflow rejection handling, implement the common default behavior in the base `Task` class and expose it as an overridable hook for custom task classes.
reason: Shares default cancel-and-notify behavior while supporting domain-specific workflows without duplicating logic in every custom task.
common_pattern: Handling and documenting workflow rejection and non-completion paths, including default behavior and overridable custom flows.

text: Translation copy utilities such as `copy_for_translation` should be composition-aware: automatically handle child-object copying for `ClusterableModel`/`InlinePanel` models and accept or detect the target page tree structure (separated or combined), instead of assuming a single layout or relying on per-model overrides.
reason: Prevents silent omission of child objects and supports both page tree layouts without duplicating special-case logic across models.
scope: Wagtail translation copying utilities, especially `copy_for_translation` for snippets/modeladmin and page trees.
common_pattern: Translation copy utilities must be composition-aware, handling structural variants such as inline child objects and page tree layout automatically rather than assuming one model/tree shape or requiring per-model overrides.

text: In the StreamField/Telepath client-side adapter interface, explicitly handle field types that cannot be populated from JavaScript — especially file uploads — rather than forcing them through the generic setState/value-setting API. Other field types should continue to be encapsulated by their adapter objects without API changes.
reason: Browsers do not allow file inputs to be populated via HTML or JavaScript, so a generic setState/serialization approach would silently fail or require hacks like base64-embedding file data in JSON. The adapter pattern remains valid for all field types that can be interfaced with through JS.
common_pattern: Client-side adapter interfaces must explicitly handle field types that JavaScript cannot populate (notably file uploads), while keeping the generic adapter pattern for all other field types.

text: For complex Wagtail admin form fields such as StreamField, design the client-side adapter API to be agnostic to submission and serialization strategy: serialize the complete field value server-side (enriched with resolved display data such as IDs mapped to edit/live URLs and titles), render it client-side via adapters instead of pre-rendering all field HTML on the server, and support both Django-style form submissions and JSON/API flows including auto-save or DRF rather than forcing one strategy or single caller model.
reason: This captures the shared principle across all three generalizations: decouple admin UI concerns from serialization/API concerns, provide enriched server-side serialization with client-side adapter rendering, and keep the adapter API flexible enough for both standard Django forms and alternative JSON/API submission strategies.
common_pattern: Designing client-side APIs for complex admin form fields (Wagtail StreamField) by separating serialization/submission strategy from admin UI rendering, serializing complete field values server-side with enriched display data, and supporting multiple form/API submission flows.

text: Before committing to a broad architectural choice or framework-wide abstraction, prototype or validate simpler/complementary implementation paths and weigh their impact on planned migrations.
reason: The two generalizations both advise considering multiple viable implementation paths before locking in a broader technical direction, especially when there is migration risk or low-cost complementary options.
common_pattern: Evaluate alternative or complementary implementation approaches—and their migration/scope impact—before committing to a broad architectural abstraction or feature direction.

text: In the Wagtail page explorer language switcher (i18n content), determine the selectable languages by the user's edit permissions across existing pages (only include languages for which the user has at least one editable page) rather than by whether the current page has a translation, and when the current page lacks a translation in the target locale, fall back to the nearest ancestor page that has one.
reason: Avoids exposing languages the user cannot edit or for which no editable page exists, while keeping navigation intuitive via an ancestor fallback.
common_pattern: Design of Wagtail/Django internationalization (i18n) language-switching UI and documentation — preferring Django's built-in i18n machinery over custom implementations, and defining how the language list is determined.

text: When extending an existing template tag, public field, widget, or API with a new data model or syntax, preserve the existing return type, output shape, field semantics, and template rendering for all existing usage. Expose the new structure or behavior only when the caller explicitly opts in via the new syntax, or keep it as an implementation detail for advanced extension.
reason: Unconditionally changing an existing public output shape or data model breaks backward compatibility and forces existing templates/callers to migrate. Gating new behavior behind opt-in syntax or implementation details keeps existing code working while still allowing the new capability.
common_pattern: Preserving backward compatibility when evolving existing public APIs and template tags: keep existing return shapes/rendering semantics unchanged for current usage, and only expose new data structures or behaviors through explicit opt-in syntax or as an implementation detail.

text: When adding background/async execution support to Wagtail hooks, do not encode a sync/async flag on hook registration; keep hooks synchronous by default and let the caller of the hook decide whether async execution is possible for that invocation.
reason: Some hooks must run synchronously or are needed synchronously by the caller. Making execution mode a fixed property of registration would break those use cases and remove caller control, whereas the caller holds the runtime context needed to decide whether blocking is required.
scope: Wagtail hook API design / background-task support
common_pattern: Both generalizations express the same API design principle: the sync/async execution mode of Wagtail hooks should be a call-site decision (controlled by the caller) rather than a property of hook registration, so that inherently synchronous hooks remain usable synchronously.

text: For derived assets that depend on page content (e.g., image renditions), do not generate them inline during the request/response cycle. Generate them during the page save/publish workflow or in a background worker; when pre-generating during publish, render the page template internally to discover all required variants.
reason: Remote storage calls (e.g., S3 fetch/store) are HTTP requests; generating many renditions inline multiplies IO, latency, and failure risk. Deferring or pre-generating reduces per-request IO and memory overhead.
scope: content-dependent derived asset generation, especially image renditions
common_pattern: Avoid generating content-dependent derived assets inline in the request/response cycle; defer generation to page save/publish workflows or background workers, optionally pre-generating during publish by rendering the page template internally to discover required variants.

text: For optional background/periodic task support, preserve existing management commands as the entry points and expose scheduling or execution mode (e.g., cron-style vs persistent process) as an option through settings.py or command flags; do not replace the commands or introduce a separate backend per execution mode.
reason: This keeps backwards compatibility, avoids backend proliferation, and provides a single worker integration path even when the underlying task queue does not natively support a given scheduling mode.
common_pattern: Extend existing management commands for optional background/periodic task execution via opt-in settings or command options, rather than replacing commands or introducing parallel backends.

text: When proposing or documenting StreamField future features (especially cross-page/cross-site copy-paste), ensure the content can be represented in a clipboard-serialisable form and validate that requirement against the planned architecture.
reason: Copy-paste interoperability depends on a portable serialisation format; validating this during roadmap/RFC review prevents building future features on an incompatible foundation.
common_pattern: StreamField roadmap features, especially cross-page/cross-site copy-paste, must be validated against a clipboard-serialisable content representation.

text: When generating multiple renditions from a single source image, load the source image into memory once and reuse that in-memory image across all rendition filters.
reason: Avoids repeated source-image I/O and reduces memory overhead during batch rendition generation.
common_pattern: Wagtail image rendition handling around source-image vs original-rendition semantics: avoid redundant source-image loading and avoid ambiguous source/original naming and documentation.

text: In image rendition APIs, clearly distinguish the source image from the original-size rendition: name any new option so it cannot be confused with `src`/`source`/`original`, and document whether the option references the source file or a rendition and which filters are allowed.
reason: The existing `src`, `source`, and `original` terminology is ambiguous for new developers, leading to trial-and-error and incorrect API use.
common_pattern: Wagtail image rendition handling around source-image vs original-rendition semantics: avoid redundant source-image loading and avoid ambiguous source/original naming and documentation.

text: When behavior depends on whether an image is animated, expose and use a dedicated `is_animated` property/check rather than relying on file extension or generic image format.
reason: Animation is orthogonal to format; for example, GIFs may be static or animated, so a format check cannot correctly distinguish animated images and may wrongly apply bypass behavior.
common_pattern: Image animation state is orthogonal to file format/extension, so behavior that depends on animation should use a dedicated animation check/property rather than inferring from format.

text: In the `willow.plugins.svgsprite` SVG plugin, expose image dimensions through a named `get_size` operation instead of making callers call the underlying `svglib`/`svgsprite` `get_box` helper directly; implement it using that existing helper rather than manually parsing SVG XML. When resolving dimensions, prioritize explicit `width`/`height` attributes on the root `<svg>` element and fall back to `viewBox` when they are absent, so viewBox-only SVGs are also supported.
reason: Keeps format-specific SVG dimension logic behind the Willow plugin API, reuses tested library behavior for edge cases and units, and correctly handles both explicit dimensions and viewBox-only SVGs with the expected precedence.
scope: Willow SVG plugin dimension handling, especially `willow.plugins.svgsprite`
common_pattern: SVG dimension resolution in Willow's svgsprite plugin: expose dimensions through a named plugin API (get_size), reuse the existing svglib/svgsprite get_box helper rather than manual XML parsing, and resolve intrinsic size by preferring explicit width/height with viewBox as fallback, including viewBox-only SVGs.

text: Prefer `__init_subclass__()` over a metaclass for subclass initialization or generating attributes/methods on subclasses, since it is simpler to understand and maintain. Use a metaclass only when `__init_subclass__()` cannot express the requirement — specifically, when dynamically generated methods are overridden in the same class body to call `super()` and therefore require an intermediate generated base class in the MRO.
reason: `__init_subclass__()` has lower cognitive overhead for the common subclass-customization case; the metaclass exception preserves the ability to construct a valid inheritance chain when generated methods must be overridable via `super()` in the same class body.
scope: Python class design and inheritance patterns
common_pattern: Python class-customization mechanism selection: prefer the simpler `__init_subclass__()` hook for subclass initialization/attribute generation, with metaclasses reserved for the specific case where an intermediate generated base class must exist in the MRO.

text: When dynamically generating class attributes via metaprogramming, keep the generated names predictable and document them or provide explicit declarations, because IDEs and static tooling may not discover dynamic attributes.
reason: This merges both generalizations into one principle: dynamic attribute generation can harm autocomplete/navigation, and the impact is mitigated by predictable naming plus documentation or explicit declarations.
common_pattern: Dynamically generated class attributes are invisible to IDEs and static tooling, so API designers should keep generated names predictable and/or document or explicitly declare them to preserve developer experience.

text: For specialized Wagtail admin display customizations (e.g., thumbnails, blank/null representations), prefer developer-side extension points — custom `wagtail.admin.ui.tables.Column` subclasses supplied via `list_display`, or model property methods — over adding dedicated core `ViewSet`/`ModelAdmin` attributes or mixins. When relying on such an extension point, document how to implement and use it.
reason: Keeps the core admin API smaller, uses existing extension mechanisms, and ensures developers can discover and adopt the intended pattern.
common_pattern: Avoid expanding core admin API for specialized display features; delegate to existing developer-side extension points (custom Column subclasses, model properties) and document them.

text: When adding a new built-in StreamField block type, follow the existing block-type conventions: name it `{Type}Block` (e.g. `ImageBlock`, matching `RichTextBlock`, `CharBlock`, `EmailBlock`), and when it semantically overlaps with an existing block type, keep its JSON serialization compatible with that type's representation so equivalent structures can be handled uniformly and refactored later.
reason: Consistent naming makes the block API predictable, while compatible serialization lets semantically equivalent block structures be handled uniformly and avoids future refactoring and migration cost.
common_pattern: New built-in StreamField block types must integrate consistently with the existing family of block types — matching both the established naming scheme and the JSON serialization shape of existing/overlapping types.

text: Design ViewSet/generic-view customization as explicit, opt-in configuration rather than implicit coupling: expose feature-specific behavior as ViewSet configuration/attributes passed into views instead of mixins on shared generic views; shared methods should accept explicit context arguments (e.g. request) and must not assume a view, request, or user is available, so they also work in non-view contexts such as chooser widgets; if view internals are required, subclass the view. Enable overriding only through an explicit allowlist with consistent signatures, not arbitrary method matching, per-variation methods, or parity-only additions.
reason: This captures the cross-PR pattern: PR #85 warns against feature-specific mixins on shared views and parity-driven API surface; PR #87 requires ViewSet shared methods to be decoupled from view internals and overrideable only explicitly.
common_pattern: ViewSet/generic-view customization should be explicit, opt-in, and decoupled from view internals: avoid feature-specific mixins, implicit view/request assumptions, arbitrary method overrides, per-variation method duplication, and parity-only additions.

text: When implementing page translations, provide a template tag that emits rel="alternate" hreflang="..." link tags for every available translation of the page, and ensure it respects each translation's published status and avoids stale cached/static output when translations are published or unpublished separately.
reason: Search engines rely on rel="alternate" hreflang links to associate translated pages, especially when translated slugs differ. A standard template tag avoids manual tracking of available languages, and respecting per-translation publishing status prevents linking to unpublished or outdated translations.
common_pattern: Page-translation features must expose SEO-friendly hreflang alternate links for all available translations through a template tag, while respecting translation publishing state.

text: For Wagtail headless support, preserve template feature parity by exposing the same data, metadata, and operations available to server-rendered templates through queryable REST API endpoints. This includes template-accessible values such as focal points, redirects, settings, snippets, and CRUD/search operations. Evaluate backend support by whether core stores the data and exposes it via API, even when the frontend renderer is implemented externally.
reason: Headless architecture separates backend data/API responsibility from frontend rendering; failing to expose template-accessible metadata or common settings/snippets creates silent parity gaps for frontend consumers.
scope: Wagtail REST API / headless support RFCs
common_pattern: Wagtail headless-support RFC/API guidance: define headless as no server-rendered HTML, evaluate backend/API responsibility separately from frontend rendering, preserve template feature parity through queryable REST API exposure, and document unsupported-feature workarounds while treating API documentation as useful but non-blocking.

text: Design resource and revision save/state APIs using standard REST semantics instead of proliferating custom action sub-endpoints: use PATCH on a status/state field (e.g. `status`, `submitted_for_moderation`) for state transitions; for create/save variants (save, save-and-publish, save-and-submit) use POST on the collection endpoint with an optional `?action=` query parameter, allowing a client to create the initial revision and immediately publish or submit it in one request. On revision save/creation endpoints accept only the `content` object in the request body, keeping revision metadata (ID, author, timestamps, moderation state) server-managed rather than submitted by clients. Reserve dedicated custom POST action endpoints for operations that do not map cleanly to CRUD or field updates (e.g. unpublish).
reason: Keeps the API surface small and predictable, matches POST semantics for create/custom actions, matches established editor behavior (e.g. Wagtail's edit views and save-revision views), and avoids clients submitting server-owned fields.
common_pattern: RESTful HTTP endpoint design for resources with state transitions/actions: prefer standard HTTP methods and field updates over proliferating custom action sub-endpoints, and keep action endpoints minimal.

text: In the revisions/moderation API, address the specific revision an action targets explicitly rather than relying on an endpoint that implicitly acts on the latest revision. Because a revision awaiting moderation may not be the latest revision, acceptance (and similar state transitions) must operate on the identified revision — either via a dedicated revision-scoped endpoint or by supplying the moderated content through the shared publish endpoint.
reason: A revision awaiting moderation is not necessarily the latest revision, so any endpoint that implicitly targets the latest version can perform the wrong operation; explicitly targeting the intended revision avoids ambiguity and incorrect state changes.
common_pattern: Designing the Wagtail admin API for page revisions and moderation workflows: how action endpoints target specific revisions, how URLs are scoped to the resource they operate on, and what belongs in the request body vs. server-managed state.

text: In permission-aware Wagtail code, resolve permission policies dynamically at request time via the central `permission_registry` (e.g., `permission_registry.get_policy(model)` in a `cached_property`) and register policy instances for models that use them. Avoid class-level policy binding, direct imports of policy instances from app modules, and viewset-specific `permission_policy` for generic foreign-key or non-page targets—use a model-agnostic permission hook when coverage must extend beyond the viewset.
reason: Covers dynamic registry lookup/registration and the complementary requirement to support non-viewset/non-page models through a model-agnostic hook.
scope: Wagtail permission registry / permission-aware views and viewsets
common_pattern: Permission policies should be resolved dynamically through the central Wagtail permission registry or model-agnostic permission hooks at request time, rather than being statically bound to views/classes or imported directly, so runtime overrides apply and authorization covers all relevant model types.

text: In Wagtail's view restriction API, pass an explicit credentials/context value to filtering and decision methods instead of reading from `HttpRequest` directly. Centralize recurring user-based restriction flows in an abstract base class (e.g., `UserPageViewRestriction`) that implements login-redirect vs permission-denied behavior, leaving concrete classes to implement only the model-level condition check.
reason: Allows access decisions and queryset filtering when no request is available (e.g., headless/API page listings) and reduces duplication across restriction types.
common_pattern: Decouple access-control logic from Django request/session internals and centralize common user-based restriction behavior in an abstract base class.

text: For collection endpoints of sub-resources, prefer a top-level flat collection with query parameters (e.g. `/api/pages/revisions/?page_id=1&author=karl`) over nesting under a single parent (e.g. `/api/pages/1/revisions/`), so that cross-resource filtering and ordering are possible.
reason: Enables cross-parent queries (e.g. admin logs, site-wide views filtered by author or date) without requiring multiple nested endpoints or extra requests.
common_pattern: API URL design must make parent-resource context explicit: sub-resource collections should be reachable across parents (flat collection + query params), and nested/detail endpoints must name their parent resource instead of relying on implicit placeholders like `-`.

text: For Wagtail/Django Admin frontend components, design widget/component interfaces and provide focused developer documentation so contributors can build common block and field widgets without needing deep knowledge of the underlying JS framework (e.g., React).
reason: A well-designed abstraction plus focused docs reduce the combined learning curve of React, Stimulus, and Wagtail-specific integration for server-side/Django developers.
scope: Wagtail admin frontend / component API design and contributor documentation
common_pattern: Complementary halves of lowering the JS-framework learning overhead for Django/Wagtail Admin widget contributors: provide a well-designed component abstraction and targeted developer documentation.

text: Support comment/annotation anchoring at any level of the content hierarchy, including nested StructBlock fields, but only where the content path is revision-stable. For structures whose child IDs are not stable across revisions (e.g., ListBlock), either implement a path re-anchoring/update-on-edit mechanism or disallow comments at that granularity.
reason: Unstable nested list-item IDs produce stale or invalid anchors, so supporting comments at unstable granularity requires a re-anchoring strategy or must be disallowed.
common_pattern: Commenting/annotation addressing in nested StreamField content must be tied to revision-stable content paths — enabling comment anchoring at any hierarchy level where addressing is reliable, and constraining or documenting granularity where it is not.

text: Use Django permission codenames (e.g. `change`, not `edit`) as the canonical action strings in the permission registry/tester mappings, and register exactly one canonical action name per `BasePermissionTester` class—do not alias the same tester under synonymous names such as both `change` and `edit`. When a permission action has distinct variants/modes (e.g. single vs. bulk, non-recursive vs. recursive), register a separate action name and tester class for each mode (e.g. `delete` and `bulk_delete`) instead of handling both modes inside one tester with a flag like `ignore_bulk`; if this would duplicate logic, have the tester access `permission_registry` and reuse the other tester rather than copying the logic.
reason: Keeps the permission API consistent with `Permission.codename` and `PermissionCheckedMixin`, avoids terminology churn, prevents ambiguous duplicate registrations, keeps bulk and non-bulk actions independently registerable/overridable, and avoids duplicated permission logic when a split is needed.
common_pattern: Design of Wagtail's permission registry API: canonical action naming tied to Django permission codenames, one tester class per action/mode, centralized mixin-aware logic, and completeness/documentation of the built-in action set.

text: In the permissions registry, keep mixin-specific permission logic inside the base permission tester classes and apply it conditionally via `isinstance()`/`issubclass()` checks, rather than registering tester classes against individual mixin classes.
reason: Models combine mixins in many ways and each mixin's permission logic may need different precedence relative to the default logic; centralizing the checks avoids infeasible registration combinations and mirrors the existing optional-features mixin pattern for generic views.
common_pattern: Design of Wagtail's permission registry API: canonical action naming tied to Django permission codenames, one tester class per action/mode, centralized mixin-aware logic, and completeness/documentation of the built-in action set.

text: Framework-adoption RFCs should prefer architectural minimalism: default to a single frontend framework unless multi-framework interop is explicitly justified with clear DOM/state ownership boundaries and hiring/training/documentation impact; avoid mandating shared abstract base controllers/global overrides until a concrete need exists; and prefer upstream framework documentation over project-specific abstraction docs.
reason: Reduces ambiguity and cognitive load from mixed frameworks, avoids premature cross-cutting abstractions, and keeps documentation maintainable by relying on upstream framework docs for standard concepts.
common_pattern: Guidance for RFCs that adopt a new frontend framework/library: make scope, trade-offs, and architectural constraints explicit before adoption.

text: When adding template override discovery for a module/feature, use a feature-level template namespace (e.g. `templates/{feature}/`) rather than nesting under an internal submodule path, and discover overrides in a cascading order from most to least specific: `{namespace}/{app_label}/{model_name}/`, then `{namespace}/{app_label}/`, then `{namespace}/`.
reason: A cascading discovery order lets developers override templates per model, per app, or globally without setting template-name attributes. A feature-level namespace keeps paths short while remaining specific enough to avoid clashes.
common_pattern: Conventions for template override discovery: use a cascading, feature-level lookup namespace and document the lookup directories and precedence.
